tb21_profile.skill: Author one precise regular expression that combines numeric range validation (month 01-12, day 01-29/31, IPv4 octet 0-255 with no leading zeros), a same-line co-occurrence condition, negative lookaround to reject alphanumeric-adjacent lookalikes, and last-match-in-line selection - and know how re.findall with MULTILINE will scan it
tb21_profile.domain: Python `re` semantics: lookahead/lookbehind, alternation for numeric ranges, anchoring, word boundaries, findall scanning order; log-file text and IPv4/ISO-date formats
tb21_profile.task_form: implement-from-spec, single artefact: write one pattern into a file that is scored on a held-out log with deliberate near-miss decoys

verifier_notes: The packet's `verifier` field and work/verifier_strength.json disagree for a few ids; verifier_strength.json is the newer pass and I used it, but for final_top10 I required non-FREE under BOTH. tw_262649 (FREE in packet, strong/0.8 in verifier_strength.json) and tw_316425, tw_316426, tw_310044, tw_147333, tw_124494 (FREE in the packet) are therefore per_source only. task_06367 (MULTILINE-without-DOTALL, a very close skill match) is FREE and excluded entirely - noted because it is the single best Terminal-Lego candidate I had to drop. Terminal-Lego's task_13817 is graded `weak` but its checker feeds a list of valid and invalid date strings and asserts the accept/reject verdict for each, so the pattern really has to be right; I kept it at rank 2 despite the grade.

TMax-15K.reason: Rows survive only if SensorID exactly matches ^[A-Z]{3}-\d{4}-[A-F0-9]{4}$; anchored strict matching against deliberately near-miss rows, like the decoys here.
Silently drop every line not matching a given POSIX ERE using regex.h; the whole score rides on getting one anchored pattern exactly right.
Validate each CSV field against a strict anchored regex (^svc-[a-z0-9]{1,10}$ and siblings); precision-of-pattern is the graded thing.
Host must match ^[a-zA-Z0-9\-]+$ and timestamp must be valid ISO8601; combines a character-class rule with date-shape validation.
Row validity requires ^SN-\d{4}$ plus a genuine ISO8601 timestamp; date validation beyond shape, which regex-log also needs for day ranges.
Use POSIX <regex.h> to validate timestamped CSV records in C; teaches ERE limits (no lookaround), the constraint behind regex-log's workarounds.
Redact exactly the substrings matching a given email ERE; getting the boundaries right decides whether neighbouring text is eaten.
Recover a log-parsing regex from a video, then apply it to the log; the task is entirely about a pattern matching a log line format.
Extract unique IPs that hit 403 across differently formatted logs; IP extraction from heterogeneous log text is the same extraction problem.
Parse [YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS] <USER_ID>: <MESSAGE> chat lines; the exact date-in-a-log-line shape, though the pattern is easy.

Recursive-Task-Synthesis.reason: Repair an email regex so domain labels neither begin nor end with a hyphen - a positional structural constraint expressed purely in the pattern.
Generate several regexes with rgxg and validate a log file with them; the same regex-plus-log pairing, though the tool writes the pattern.
Email regex that must accept a `+` in the local part while rejecting four other fixed strings; accept/reject boundary tuning.
One regex with a backreference forcing a consistent separator, results emitted as JSON captures; cross-position constraints in a single pattern.
Email-validation regex in a runnable script; pattern authoring at the easiest level.
Phone-number regex with a repeated-separator backreference; same family, no range validation.
Duplicate-family phone-number regex; listed because RTS has no deeper regex content.
Export a single backreference-bearing regex as a module; pure pattern authoring, trivial scope.
Another phone-number regex variant in the same cluster.
Find a date in a hidden file and normalise it to YYYY-MM-DD; date-format handling only, no pattern to design.

TerminalWorld-Seeds-Clean.reason: Write one regular expression that classifies four specific email strings correctly; accept/reject tuning, but graded FREE in the packet.
Extract the unique IPv4 addresses from DNS records, filtering by record type so hostnames are not mistaken for addresses - the same lookalike problem.
Generate regexes with rgxg and reproduce their exact output; regex construction rather than use. Packet says FREE, verifier_strength.json says strong - unresolved.
Find lines consisting entirely of space characters: a fully anchored whole-line pattern where a missing anchor silently over-matches.
Regex to extract the name before a comma; single-capture extraction, small.
Regex for consecutive Hangul runs versus individual characters; character-class and quantifier precision.
Single regex validating North American phone formats; FREE-graded in both sources, so per_source only.
Match filenames against a glob and grep file contents; pattern matching, but shell globs rather than regex semantics.
Filter out comment and empty lines from a source file; line-level predicate, near-zero regex depth.
Clojure last-element exercise; unrelated, present only to fill the quota - TerminalWorld has no substantive regex task.

SWE-Smith-Seeds-Clean.reason: looks_like_ip wrongly accepts strings with newlines and malformed octets - exactly regex-log's IPv4 false-positive and anchoring problem.
The candump log-line regex fails when R/T flags trail the line; fixing a pattern against real log text with unexpected suffixes.
Uses match instead of fullmatch with a wrong pattern when parsing tool output lines; match-versus-search-versus-fullmatch is the anchoring trap here.
parse_date breaks on dates without a sign; ISO date-shape parsing built from regex alternatives, the date half of this task.
A missing pair of parentheses in an HTML-tag regex changes grouping and breaks parsing; group-structure bugs are the commonest hand-written-regex defect.
Preprocessor directives missed when not at line start or spanning lines; line-anchor and multiline behaviour, which MULTILINE makes live here.
Operator ordering in a lexer regex alternation decides which branch wins; the same first-alternative-wins hazard as numeric range alternations.
DateTimeParser's _input_re_map, the table of regexes for each date token; exposure to how date formats decompose into patterns.
TextFSM parses text with an ordered rule set of regexes; log-text extraction driven entirely by pattern correctness.
find_all mishandles compiled regex objects; only the regex-API surface transfers, not pattern design.

SWE-Rebench-Tasks-Clean.reason: An FTP listing regex false-matches when a filename contains AM or PM - the same unanchored-context false positive regex-log's decoys create.
A pattern filter only matches at the start of the string because of match-versus-search; anchoring semantics decide the whole result.
Fix a regex that escapes non-special characters; escaping and metacharacter handling, where a stray backslash silently changes the language.
X-Forwarded-For parsing must handle bracketed IPv6 alongside IPv4; separating real addresses from lookalike text in a header.
Multiple regex converters in one route mix up captured parameters; group numbering and ordering inside a composed pattern.
A converter regex containing `/` changes how much of the path it may consume; reasoning about what a subpattern is allowed to match.
AllowedPattern validation rejects legitimate parameters; a validation regex applied where it should not be.
Content-Length validation does not handle surrounding spaces; strict field-shape checking in a text protocol, the same whitespace-boundary care.
Version-specifier grammar parsed by regex; precise pattern semantics over a small formal language.
An unclosed tag inside a code span confuses regex-based inline parsing; context-sensitivity that a flat pattern cannot express.

Terminal-Lego-15k.reason: Write an extended regex that validates IPv4: four octets 0-255 with no leading zeros and no stray adjacent characters. Half of the TB2.1 pattern, verbatim.
Regex date validator enforcing month and day ranges and rejecting invalid dates; the other half of the TB2.1 pattern, including the 29-day question.
One regex that requires two substrings in any order via lookahead - the construction needed to demand an IPv4 and a date on the same line.
Negative lookahead for 'not followed by' in grep, including why BRE cannot do it; the assertion that rejects alphanumeric-adjacent lookalikes.
Debug and repair several broken complex regexes; exactly the iterate-against-counterexamples loop the TB2.1 task is scored on.
Extend ^/[a-z0-9]+$ to exclude specific words without breaking the rest; adding an exclusion assertion to a working pattern.
Why re.findall skips overlapping matches and how to get them; the findall scanning rule that decides which date in a line is returned.
Match 'foo' only when not followed by 'bar'; a clean negative-lookahead drill on the exact assertion regex-log needs.
Emulate (?<!filename)\.js$ where lookbehind is unavailable; forces understanding what a lookbehind actually asserts.
Match and rewrite the last octet of IPv4 addresses in nginx access logs; IPv4 patterns applied to real log lines.

CalibForge.reason: The grep regex misses some valid emails in the sample files; repair one pattern until it accepts every real case - the same debug-a-pattern loop.
Diagnose and fix correctness bugs in an NFA regex matcher; you cannot do it without knowing precisely what each construct should match.
Implement a grep -E subset in C over real files and lines; line-oriented matching with the ERE feature set this task's patterns live in.
Build a regex engine that cannot blow up on a?a?a?...aaa; teaches why nested optional alternations backtrack, which range alternations invite.
NFA matching engine with no backtracking allowed; exact semantics of alternation and closure learned by implementing them.
Regex engine from scratch used as a line filter over stdin; mirrors how the TB2.1 pattern is applied to log text.
Whole-input anchored matching in a hand-written C regex engine; anchoring semantics from the implementer's side.
Parse an event log with multiline records and several timestamp formats; disambiguating date shapes inside messy log text.
Parse Apache combined logs, extracting IP and timestamp per line while skipping malformed lines; the same fields and the same decoys.
Analyse three access-log formats, one with malformed entries, into an incident report; robust log-line extraction across formats.

final_top10.reason: Extended regex validating IPv4 as four 0-255 octets with no leading zeros and no stray adjacent characters - literally half of the required pattern.
Regex date validator enforcing month and day ranges and rejecting invalid dates - the other half, including the 29-day February question.
One regex requiring two substrings in any order via lookahead: the construction needed to demand an IPv4 and a date on the same line.
Negative lookahead for 'not followed by', including why BRE cannot express it - the assertion that rejects alphanumeric-adjacent lookalikes.
looks_like_ip accepts strings with embedded newlines and malformed octets: exactly the IPv4 false-positive and anchoring failure this task punishes.
Debug and repair several broken complex regexes - the same iterate-against-counterexamples loop the TB2.1 task is scored on.
A grep regex misses valid emails in the sample files; repair the single pattern until every real case is matched and no decoy is.
An FTP listing regex false-matches when a filename contains AM or PM - the unanchored-context false positive the TB2.1 decoys are built from.
Explains why re.findall skips overlapping matches: the scanning rule that decides which date on a line the harness actually returns.
Extend a working anchored pattern with an exclusion for specific words without breaking the rest; adding an assertion to a live regex.

notes: Terminal-Lego-15k decisively wins this task and takes six of the final ten. It is built from StackOverflow regex questions and the TB2.1 task is a StackOverflow-grade regex puzzle: it contains a dedicated IPv4-validation-by-regex task, a date-validation-by-regex task, three negative-lookahead tasks, a lookbehind-emulation task, a regex-debugging task and a re.findall-overlap task. Nothing in the v1 pool is close - `search tmax "lookahead|lookbehind"` returns zero matches across 14,601 TMax tasks, and TMax's 496 IP hits and 328 regex hits are all log-parsing chores where the pattern is handed to the solver. CalibForge helps but in a different direction: its regex content is engine implementation (six separate build-a-regex-engine tasks, all strong-verified), which teaches semantics rather than authoring, so it earns one top-ten slot. SWE-Smith and SWE-Rebench contribute unusually well here for bug-fix corpora because regex bugs are their own genre: tldextract's IP validator and pyfilesystem's AM/PM false positive are the two best false-positive lessons in the whole pool. Recursive-Task-Synthesis and TerminalWorld cannot field 10 defensible candidates; RTS has only the duplicated email/phone regex families and TerminalWorld's best entries are FREE-graded one-liners, so both lists bottom out around overall 2. One casualty of the FREE rule worth recording: Terminal-Lego task_06367 is about using re.MULTILINE without re.DOTALL - the exact flag combination this task runs under - but its verifier is FREE.
